_readme: Cache-first lookup content for the 15 suggested chip questions defined in frontend/app.html's DOMAINS array.

WIRED (demo cache-first path, both personas): app.services.chortlechat loads this file into _PRESET_CACHE (keyed by exact question text) and, on a cache hit, answers straight from baseline_answer or banter_answer below, whichever the request's persona asked for — no retrieval call, no confidence-threshold gate, no generation call for either persona. All 15 questions are covered, so a demo run never depends on a live vector store or instruct model for any of the suggested chips. See app.services.chortlechat's module docstring, _PRESET_CACHE, and _preset_response.

Every baseline_answer is drafted strictly from the cited passage(s) in backend/data/chortlechat_corpus.json, in Baseline's voice, using the same 'say only what the source supports' rule app.services.chortlechat._BASELINE_PROMPT already enforces. All doc_id/domain citations below were re-verified directly against chortlechat_corpus.json.

Every banter_answer is a hand-drafted restyle of that same entry's baseline_answer, written under the exact same rule app.services.chortlechat._BANTER_PROMPT enforces at generation time: personality and phrasing may differ, but every fact, number, and claim must already be present in baseline_answer. Nothing in banter_answer should ever say more, or something different, than baseline_answer already says — treat any drift caught in review as a bug in the draft, not an acceptable embellishment.

Each banter_answer opens with an actual short joke (a setup/punchline one-liner or pun) tied to that entry's topic, in the style of the r/Jokes-derived 'Short Jokes' dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Fraser/short-jokes), before restating the same facts baseline_answer gives. The joke itself is original, not sourced from that dataset — it's a style reference, not a text reuse — and it never carries a factual claim of its own; the facts still only ever come from baseline_answer.

confidence is deliberately null on every entry, not a filled-in number, and stays null in the AskResponse for a cache hit too — the same meaning it already carries for 'nothing was retrieved,' which is literally true here since retrieval never runs for a cache hit.

summary.note_on_count: frontend's DOMAINS array lists 18 chip slots across 6 tabs, but 'All' repeats 5 questions that also appear under their own domain tab, so there are only 15 distinct question strings. All 15 are covered here.

entries.question: What ocean heat conditions favor tropical cyclone intensification?
entries.baseline_answer: According to nasa-smd-50#chunk0, tropical cyclone intensification in the central Bay of Bengal is favored by a barrier layer thickness of 10-30 meters combined with a tropical cyclone heat potential of 40-80 kJ/cm². As storm intensity increases, the right-rear sector shows the largest heat-potential anomalies, and sea-surface cooling beneath the strongest, slowest-moving storms reaches 0.5-1.2°C in the inner core.
entries.banter_answer: Why did the tropical cyclone break up with the shallow ocean? Because it needed something with real depth! Per nasa-smd-50#chunk0, a 10-30 meter barrier layer sitting on 40-80 kJ/cm² of stored heat acts like high-octane rocket fuel for central Bay of Bengal storms. The growing cyclone treats the right-rear sector like its personal all-you-can-eat buffet, leaving behind a chilly 0.5-1.2°C sea-surface brain freeze right under its slowest, angriest core.

entries.question: How does eyewall mesovortex dynamics affect a hurricane's intensity?
entries.baseline_answer: Based on nasa-smd-10#chunk0, eyewall mesovortices in Hurricane Ike showed a consistent structure of vorticity and vertical-velocity maxima wherever they formed. These mesovortices continued forming after the storm moved inland, though their structure altered as the storm interacted with the coastline and weakened. The source documents structural dynamics rather than quantifying net impacts on peak intensity.
entries.banter_answer: What do you call a hurricane's eyewall doing the exact same dance move on loop? A mesovortex going full breakdance! According to nasa-smd-10#chunk0, Hurricane Ike's mesovortices were total creatures of habit, locking into the exact same vorticity and vertical-velocity routine everywhere they spun. They even crashed the party inland post-landfall, though tripping over the coastline forced them to awkward-shuffle as the storm weakened. Don't ask how many extra horsepower that gave Ike's peak intensity though, because the source completely forgot to track that score!
entries.caveat: Source documents mesovortex structure and behavior, not a quantified link to intensity. Answer is scoped to say only that.

entries.question: What atmospheric conditions influence tropical cyclone formation?
entries.baseline_answer: Tropical cyclone formation requires warm ocean surface temperatures (at least 26.5°C to a depth of ~50m), high mid-tropospheric humidity, atmospheric instability, low vertical wind shear, a pre-existing low-level disturbance, and sufficient Coriolis force (at least 5° away from the equator).
entries.banter_answer: What is a tropical cyclone's absolute favorite recipe? A piping-hot ocean bath with a massive pinch of chaotic humidity! For a storm to cook up, it demands sea temperatures of at least 26.5°C down to 50 meters, a super-moist mid-troposphere, and an atmospheric setup unstable enough to throw a tantrum. It also needs minimal wind shear so its chimney doesn't get chopped off, a pre-existing low-level disturbance to get the party started, and enough distance from the equator for the Coriolis force to give it a proper spin!

entries.question: How does airborne Saharan dust affect tropical cyclone development?
entries.baseline_answer: According to nasa-smd-80#chunk0 and nasa-smd-90#chunk0, the Saharan Air Layer suppresses Atlantic tropical cyclones by introducing dry, stable air that increases vertical wind shear and lower-level temperature inversions. Concurrently, dust particles act as cloud condensation and ice nuclei, altering hydrometeor properties, diabatic heating, and thermodynamic structure (as observed in Hurricane Erin in 2001). The net balance between suppression and microphysical influence remains unresolved.
entries.banter_answer: Why did the hurricane avoid the Saharan Air Layer? Because it couldn't handle that dry humor! As exposed in nasa-smd-80#chunk0 and nasa-smd-90#chunk0, this dusty blanket acts like the ultimate party pooper by dumping dry air, cranking up wind shear, and slamming the brakes on storm growth with thermal inversions. Yet its sneaky dust grains double as cloud-building ice nuclei, secretly rewiring heating patterns and cloud structures like a rogue technician did to Hurricane Erin back in 2001. Scientists are still locked in a heated feud over whether the party-pooper effect or the cloud-tinkering wins the match!

entries.question: What is the impact of Saharan dust on the atmosphere?
entries.baseline_answer: As cited in nasa-smd-85#chunk0 and nasa-smd-86#chunk0, approximately 240 ± 80 million tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic annually. This dust impacts the Earth's radiative balance directly through sunlight absorption and scattering. Furthermore, dust coated with sulfur or soluble material functions as cloud condensation and ice nuclei, modifying cloud development.
entries.banter_answer: What did the Saharan dust say to the Atlantic Ocean? Catch you on the flip side for our annual road trip! As spilled in nasa-smd-85#chunk0 and nasa-smd-86#chunk0, a massive 240 ± 80 million tons of dust take this transatlantic frequent-flyer flight every single year. Once airborne, this floating circus plays pinball with incoming sunlight, and any dust wearing a sulfur coat moonlights as a undercover cloud seed to hijack local cloud production!

entries.question: How are dust storms characterized by particle size?
entries.baseline_answer: According to nasa-smd-25#chunk0, dust storms are evaluated via MODIS spectral reflectance rather than direct physical particle sizing. Dust reflectance increases across wavelengths from 0.4 to 2.5 μm, reaching a minimum in MODIS band 3 and a maximum in band 7, establishing a spectral signature distinct from clouds in satellite imagery.
entries.banter_answer: Why don't meteorologists use tiny microscopes on giant dust storms? Because satellites prefer reading their flashiest outfit colors instead! Per nasa-smd-25#chunk0, scientists don't pull out the tape measure for individual dust grains; they let MODIS watch how dust reflects light as it climbs from 0.4 to 2.5 μm (flooring it at band 3 and peaking at band 7). That unique glowing fingerprint lets space cameras call out 'dust storm!' without ever touching a microscopic grain of sand!
entries.caveat: Source characterizes dust by spectral reflectance signature (via MODIS bands), not by a particle-size distribution as literally asked.

entries.question: How are historical droughts reconstructed from climate data?
entries.baseline_answer: Based on nasa-smd-30#chunk0, historical drought reconstruction requires correcting precipitation records for non-climatic biases, such as snowfall-to-liquid conversion errors, wind-induced rain gauge collection losses, evaporation between readings, and instrumentation changes. Because undercounting is most severe during cold seasons, reconstructions are primarily restricted to warm months (April–August) using screened high-quality records.
entries.banter_answer: Why did the historical rain gauge get sent to history rehab? Because its story was leaking more lies than actual water! As exposed in nasa-smd-30#chunk0, climate sleuths have to scrub out massive historical blunders like broken snow-melting math, wind blowing rain past the bucket, sneaky evaporation theft, and vintage hardware upgrades. Winter gauges are practically professional pinocchios, so researchers banish cold-season data entirely and only let pristine April-to-August records into the VIP club!

entries.question: How is satellite-based precipitation data validated on the ground?
entries.baseline_answer: According to nasa-smd-15#chunk0, GPM satellite precipitation estimates are validated by comparing radar and imager data against quality-controlled ground instruments (NPOL radar, high-resolution rain-rate radar, disdrometers, and rain gauges). To account for a 0–30 minute surface fall-delay lag following overpasses, retrievals in this study were evaluated against ground measurements averaged 2–8 minutes post-overpass.
entries.banter_answer: Why was the raindrops' flight delayed on arrival? Because gravity forgot to give them a fast pass for the 30-minute drop! As spilled in nasa-smd-15#chunk0, fancy GPM satellite scans get audited by ground snitches like NPOL radar, high-res rain gizmos, disdrometers, and plain ol' rain buckets. Since falling rain takes anywhere up to half an hour to actually hit the dirt after the satellite flashes its camera, researchers graded orbit scores against ground averages clocked 2 to 8 minutes after the flyby!

entries.question: What evidence do scientists use to study climate change over time?
entries.baseline_answer: As demonstrated in nasa-smd-110#chunk0 and nasa-smd-111#chunk0, scientists utilize long-term statistical trend analysis, such as applying the Mann-Kendall test to decades of spring water metrics. This methodology enabled researchers to link decreasing spring discharge to declining precipitation trends while isolating water quality degradation caused by human activities like mining, agriculture, and urbanization.
entries.banter_answer: What is a climate scientist's absolute favorite detective tool? A statistical math test that catches environmental suspects red-handed! As demonstrated in nasa-smd-110#chunk0 and nasa-smd-111#chunk0, researchers put decades of spring water stats through the Mann-Kendall lie-detector test to pin shrinking spring flow straight on drying skies. Meanwhile, the exact same math busted human mining, dirty farming, and sprawling cities for poisoning the local water supply!
entries.caveat: Reused from a water-quality case study rather than a general treatment of climate-change evidence, since the corpus has no passage framed at that general level.

entries.question: What environmental factors drive wildland fire risk?
entries.baseline_answer: According to nasa-smd-35#chunk0, wildland fires contribute approximately 25% of primary PM2.5 emissions in the US. Regional ignition sources vary: prescribed and agricultural burns account for most ignitions in the southeastern US, whereas lightning ignites about 70% of burned area in the western US. Burned area extent in both regions remains strongly linked to atmospheric environmental conditions and climatic variability.
entries.banter_answer: Who gets caught holding the match when wildland fires start blazing? The Southeast points at humans, the West blames Zeus's lightning, and the smoky air chokes on 25% of America's finest PM2.5 soot! According to nasa-smd-35#chunk0, prescribed farm fires rule the East while lightning strikes torch 70% of the West's burn zones. But no matter who sparked the match, climate conditions and dry weather are the real evil geniuses pulling the strings behind total scorched earth!

entries.question: What causes environmental degradation?
entries.baseline_answer: Based on nasa-smd-0#chunk0 and nasa-smd-66#chunk0, pollution is the primary driver of environmental degradation. Primary sources include vehicle emissions, agricultural runoff, industrial chemical spills, and poorly managed natural resource harvesting, leading to resource depletion, ecosystem disruption, and wildlife population declines.
entries.banter_answer: Why did Mother Nature hire a full-time hitman? Because pollution keeps wrecking her neighborhood like a wrecking ball on loose hinges! As exposed in nasa-smd-0#chunk0 and nasa-smd-66#chunk0, pollution is public enemy number one, blasting ecosystems through belching tailpipes, toxic farm runoff, messy factory spills, and greedy resource harvesting. The horrific collateral damage leaves natural resources bankrupt, habitats scrambled, and local wildlife running for their lives!

entries.question: How does pollution affect water quality?
entries.baseline_answer: As detailed in nasa-smd-110#chunk0 and nasa-smd-112#chunk0, long-term monitoring of a karst spring in China using the Mann-Kendall trend test showed that anthropogenic pollution—specifically coal mining, quarrying, agriculture, and urbanization—caused measurable water-quality degradation over decades. Concurrently, climate-linked precipitation declines reduced total spring discharge.
entries.banter_answer: Why did the historic Chinese spring fail its medical checkup? Because it was drowning in decades of human filth! As detailed in nasa-smd-110#chunk0 and nasa-smd-112#chunk0, the Mann-Kendall trend test acted like a ruthless judge, proving coal mines, stone quarries, agricultural sludge, and urban sprawl systematically ruined water purity over time. And to add insult to injury, dropping rain levels left the poor spring completely gasping for flow!

entries.question: What causes severe mesoscale thunderstorm systems?
entries.baseline_answer: According to nasa-smd-5#chunk0, high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) severe convection accounts for most cool-season nocturnal tornadoes and damaging wind events. Regional mechanisms differ: western US HSLC systems typically involve lower-tropospheric dryness combined with surface triple points or terrain upslope forcing, whereas eastern systems develop along warm sectors or cold fronts with lower cloud bases despite similar upper-level forcing.
entries.banter_answer: What do you call a violent thunderstorm that strikes strictly after bedtime when the weather alarms are fast asleep? A ninja of severe weather! As exposed in nasa-smd-5#chunk0, high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) convection is the sneaky criminal behind cool-season night tornadoes and destructive wind blasts. Out West, it loves bone-dry lower air paired with surface triple points, while back East, it sneaks in under low clouds riding cold or warm fronts like a master thief!
entries.caveat: Source characterizes high-shear, low-CAPE (HSLC) severe convection regionally rather than stating a general causal mechanism for severe mesoscale thunderstorms.

entries.question: What is a dryline and how does it trigger severe weather?
entries.baseline_answer: Based on nasa-smd-130#chunk0, a dryline is a boundary separating dry air from a moist air mass. Drylines act as convective triggers for severe thunderstorms; in subtropical southern Africa (specifically eastern South Africa), they occur most frequently during early summer, coinciding with peak occurrences of large hail and damaging winds.
entries.banter_answer: What's the driest breakup line in the entire atmosphere? A dryline—it cuts bone-dry air from muggy air and starts a full-blown thunderstorm brawl just for fun! Per nasa-smd-130#chunk0, this dramatic air boundary acts as the ultimate launchpad for explosive storms. Over eastern South Africa in early summer, drylines pop up constantly, ushering in huge golf-ball hail and roof-ripping windstorms like clockwork!

entries.question: What is cold-air damming?
entries.baseline_answer: As described in nasa-smd-125#chunk0, cold-air damming occurs when cold, dense air banks against mountain slopes. A documented Appalachian case study showed a stationary surface anticyclone paired with a low-pressure system east of Jackson, Mississippi, intensifying the mountain-parallel pressure gradient. This setup produced increased ridging east of the crests (Virginia to Georgia) and troughing to the west (New York to Tennessee).
entries.banter_answer: What do you call freezing cold air slammed against mountain peaks with nowhere to run? A massive atmospheric traffic jam that refuses to merge! As detailed in nasa-smd-125#chunk0, a parked high-pressure monster and a low-pressure slider near Mississippi squished heavy freezing air directly against the Appalachians. This epic pressure squeeze piled high ridging from Virginia down to Georgia while carving out deep troughing from New York over to Tennessee!
entries.caveat: Source is a specific case study (a March 22 synoptic event) rather than a textbook definition; the answer describes the phenomenon through that case.
